notes.text: 1 H E following dialogue is no less remarkable for the mafterly manner of its composition, than for the different effects which the perufal of it is related to have formerly produced. For the arguments which it contains for the immortality of the soul, are said to have mcited Cleombrotus to suicide, and to have difluaded Olympiodorus, an eminent Platonic philosopher, from its perpetration. Indeed, it is by no means wonderful that a person like Cleombrotus, ignorant (es his conduct evinces) that the death so much inculcated in this dialogue is a philosophic, and not a natural death, should be led to an action which is in most cases highly criminal. This ignorance however is not peculiar to Cleombrotus, since I am afraid there are scarcely any of the prelent day who know that it is one thing for the soul to be separated from the body, and another for the body to be separated from the soul, and that the former is by no means a necessary consequence of the latter.

For it is necessary in things of this kind either to learn or to discover the manner of their subsistence; or, if both these are impossible, then by receiving the best of human reasons, and that which is the most difficult of confutation, to venture upon this as on a rest, and fail in it through the ocean of life, unless feme one should be able to be carried more safely and with less danger by means of a firmer vehicle, or a certain olivine rea/on,'* Here, in the iirfl: place, it must be observed, that it is Simmias vi'ho thus speaks, an imperfect disciple of his great mailer, as is evident from many parts of this dialogue, and not Socrates himself. And, in the next place, though it should be urged that Socrates himself is here said by Simmias to have admitted that " to know these particulars clearly in the present life is either impossible or a thing very difficult to obtain," it must be observed, that Socrates thus speaks from a deep conviction that this sublime truth, the immortality of the soul, could not be fully comprehended by his auditors, who were very far from being masters in philosophy, and that this must be the case with the multitude in general. Hence, he says, it is either impossible or very difficult to obtain this knowledge. — To the multitude it is impossible, and to the fe%v very difficult, because it requires many preparatory disciplines, and a genius naturally adapted to sublime speculations.
